title: VoyageReplay scenario (.voyage.json)
description: A timestamped reconstruction of a marine incident or manoeuvre, sufficient to replay it in 3D from any participant's viewpoint. Format version 0.1 is UNSTABLE and may change without a migration.

formatVersion.description: Semver-ish version of this format. 0.x is unstable.

occurredAt.description: ISO 8601 with offset. For a collision, the moment of contact.

timeZone.description: IANA zone the human-readable clock in this scenario refers to.

locality.description: Free text, e.g. 'Suo-nada, off Nojima, Yamaguchi'.

license.description: Terms the underlying source data is reproduced under.

origin.description: Geodetic origin of the local tangent plane. All rendering happens in metres east/north of this point, so it should sit near the action - a few kilometres out, the flat-earth error is far below the precision of the source data.

lightCondition.description: Whether navigation lights would be exhibited and visible. 'night' and 'restricted-visibility' both mean lights are shown.

visibilityMetres.description: Meteorological visibility. null when the source does not state it.

waves.description: Figures for the sea, as against the sea state class, which is a different kind of statement. 'derivation' is required for the same reason it is on a track point: a height reconstructed from testimony is not a measurement, and a reconstruction that cannot tell them apart cannot be checked.

significantHeightMetres.description: Significant wave height: the mean of the highest third. Individual waves run well above it - the highest tenth averages 1.27 times this, and the largest of an hour's waves about 1.9 times. Bounded above because the arithmetic downstream stops returning numbers long before the type does; the highest ever measured is 19 m.

peakPeriodSeconds.description: Period of the spectral peak. Assumed from the height where absent, which runs long in fetch-limited water.

fromDegreesTrue.description: Direction the waves come FROM, degrees true - the convention reports use.

wind.description: The one weather figure a deck log always has. A wind sea runs with the wind, so this settles a wave direction the sea state cannot give - though swell runs from wherever its storm was, so a stated wave direction still wins. Fully developed, the wind gives an UPPER bound on the height, not the height: a sea under a rising wind is smaller than the wind can eventually raise.

fromDegreesTrue.description: Direction the wind blows FROM, the convention reports use.

speedKnots.description: Mean wind speed. Bounded above well past anything a merchant ship reports being under way in.

beaufortForce.description: Where a report gives a force rather than a speed, which is common. A force is a class and not a figure - 5 is 17 to 21 knots - so it is carried as one, and never collapsed to a midpoint.

current.description: Set (degrees true, the direction the water flows TOWARD) and drift (knots).

marks.description: Sea marks: buoys and the like. Separate from actors because they do not move, carry no track and have no derivation of motion to argue about - a moored buoy is a place, not a passage. Which side of one a ship passed is often the question a report is answering.

kind.description: Whether it floats or is built. A buoy is moored and rides the sea, and the position given is her SINKER's - she lies somewhere on a circle about it. A beacon stands on a foundation on the shoal it marks: it does not move, and its position is its own.

shape.description: IALA buoy shapes, which carry meaning: a can is port hand, a cone starboard, a sphere safe water. Optional, because reports often omit it - a renderer then has to choose one, and what it chose is named beside the mark rather than declared here, so that the shape drawn and the shape stated cannot drift apart.

colour.description: The body's colour. Solid colours only for now; banded and striped marks carry meaning this format cannot yet state.

heightMetres.description: Body height ABOVE THE WATER, excluding any topmark, and the same datum for both kinds. A buoy stands above her own waterline. A beacon continues below the sea to a foundation whose depth nothing in this format states - so a height measured from that foundation, which is what a light list gives as the structure height, could not be placed against the water at all. The part above the water is the figure the picture and a sightline both need. Buoys are small compared with an ocean wave and follow the surface closely, which is what makes one the plainest way to see a sea.

light.description: The light the mark carries. ABSENT MEANS THE FILE DID NOT SAY, not that the mark was unlit - a buoy and a lighted buoy are different marks, and so are a beacon and a light beacon, but a report omitting the light is the ordinary case. Its rhythm is what identifies the mark: under IALA the four cardinal marks are told apart by nothing else.

character.description: The Light List abbreviation - "Fl(2) W 10s", "Q(6)+LFl 15s", "Iso W 4s", "Mo(A) W 7s". The classes are those of IALA Recommendation E-110 Table 2: F, Oc, Iso, Fl, LFl, Q, VQ, UQ, Mo, Al and OcAl, with an optional group or composite group in brackets, an optional colour (W, R, G, Y, Bu) and an optional period in seconds.

phases.description: The actual on/off durations, where the source gives them. THE ABBREVIATION DOES NOT FIX THEM: "Fl 4s" says one flash in every four seconds and not how long the flash is, so a sequence worked out from the abbreviation alone conforms to E-110 without being the sequence that light showed. State these and they are used instead, and the page says which it had.

colour.description: The colour shown in this phase. Absent is darkness.

mooring.description: What a buoy swings on. Only meaningful for one that floats, and stated so that the watch circle can be given as a figure rather than left to a reader who does not know it is there - at 20 m depth on three times scope it is 57 m, a ship's length of slack.

chainScope.description: Length of chain as a multiple of the depth. Two to three is usual.

then.$comment: IALA body shapes carry meaning - a can is port hand, a cone starboard - and a beacon has no equivalent: its form is engineering, and belongs to a vocabulary this format does not yet have. Letting one be stated and then ignored would lie to whoever wrote it.
A beacon is not moored. It stands on a foundation and has no watch circle.

derivation.description: Where this figure came from. This is the claim the reconstruction rests on, so it is required rather than optional: 'measured' is a recording, 'digitised' was read off a plotted chart, 'inferred' was reconstructed from testimony or narrative, 'interpolated' was computed by this tool between other points.

citation.description: Human-readable pointer precise enough to check by hand, e.g. 'Appendix table 1, p.14'.

id.description: Stable within the scenario. Reports usually anonymise as A / B; keep that.

kind.description: Discriminator. Only 'vessel' is implemented; the field exists so other actor kinds can be added without a format break.

type.description: Drives which lights are exhibited and the default hull shape.

referencePointOffsets.description: Where the reported position actually sits on the hull. AIS message 5 carries exactly these four distances, and JTSB appendix tables restate them in a footnote - so a track reported at the GPS antenna can be moved to the ship's centre without guessing.

positionAt.description: What the lat/lon in each point refers to. AIS reports the GPS antenna, which on a 180 m ship is over a hundred metres from the bow - close enough to matter when the question is whether the hulls touched. "reference-point" means the positions have already been moved onto the ship's own reference point, her centre, so a consumer must not apply referencePointOffsets to them a second time.

t.description: ISO 8601 with offset. Verbose on purpose: a reconstruction is checked by a human against a report that prints wall-clock times.

cogDegreesTrue.description: Course over ground. Where the ship is GOING.

headingDegreesTrue.description: Where the bow POINTS. Absent whenever the source could not supply it - a Class B AIS transponder does not transmit heading at all, and half of a two-ship reconstruction typically lacks it. Do not silently substitute cogDegreesTrue: the difference is the drift angle, and in a tideway it is visible.

derivation.description: Overrides the track's derivation for this point alone.
